evening.title: NITI Aayog Launches New Framework to Measure Science and Technology Development
evening.text:
NITI Aayog on Tuesday launched the “India S&T Scoreboard” as an interactive platform that provides an integrated view of the science & technology landscape of states and UTs, bringing together data on the science and technology ecosystem, including higher education institutions, R&D institutions, deep tech startups, and incubators, along with S&T outputs like research publications and patents.
NITI Aayog Vice Chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri emphasised that India’s further progress in science and technology requires a more active role by the states. He noted that the Scoreboard will help states identify their strengths and gaps, learn from one another, and design better programmes and policies in science and technology. He urged all states and UTs to make full use of the platform.
Going beyond the volume of output, the scoreboard presents indicators of research quality, impact, collaboration and open access across priority research areas and three sectors, namely Academia, Government R&D Labs, and Industry. It also enables side-by-side comparison of states and UTs and provides detailed state profiles, including state policies and best practices.
Developed as a key NITI Aayog initiative, the Scoreboard has been designed to facilitate evidence-based policymaking and benchmarking across states and UTs.
NITI Aayog’s Senior Adviser Prof Vivek Kumar Singh said that the Scoreboard has been built to go beyond the volume of output and capture quality, impact and collaboration, so that states can identify expertise and areas for focused action.
Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, Umesh V. Waghmare, noted that the Scoreboard adds a valuable state-level picture to the national evidence base on science and technology, and highlighted the role of state S&T Councils and state universities in widening India’s research base.
Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences, T. Srinivasa Kumar underscored that earth sciences are closely linked to every state, and that local capacity in science and technology is essential for states to make effective use of forecasts, early warnings and opportunities in the ocean sector.
NITI Aayog’s Member, S&T, Prof Abhay Karandikar emphasised that sound policy in science and technology must rest on reliable and comparable evidence. He observed that data on research and innovation has so far remained fragmented across multiple sources, making it difficult for states to assess where they stand. The Scoreboard addresses this gap by bringing ecosystem, publication and patent data together on a single interactive dashboard, with trends over years, so that states can track their progress over time.
The launch was followed by a walkthrough of the Scoreboard and a technical session on its methodology and data sources. Representatives of states noted that the platform will support their planning and help build institutional capacity and skilled human resources in science and technology at the state level.
(IANS)

evening.title: Boffins use machine-learning tricks to create a starlight dimmer switch
evening.text:
Scientists have developed a way to remove starlight from telescope images that improved sensitivity to faint exoplanets by up to 15 times in tests on James Webb Space Telescope data.

A team led by Northwestern University's Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez combined a physics-based telescope model with optimization techniques used in machine learning to subtract unwanted starlight.

Directly imaging exoplanets remains difficult because their host stars' glare can overwhelm their faint light. Existing techniques subtract modeled or reference starlight, but tiny changes in telescope optics can leave residual glare that hides planets.

The team's Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP) framework models how light passes through the telescope, adjusts for optical imperfections, and simulates the glare to be subtracted.

Applied to observations from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), FLIP produced the first image of the known giant planet 51 Eridani b at an infrared wavelength of 4.3 micrometers, where conventional processing had failed. Tests showed sensitivity improvements of two to 15 times over conventional techniques, according to the Nature paper.

"This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories… potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success," the paper says.

Further work includes reducing computational demands and developing ways to handle the much larger data volumes produced by ground-based observations.

The researchers hope further development and testing will bring direct images of Earth-like planets closer, while reducing the extent to which tiny telescope instabilities obscure them. ®

evening.title: Safran Secures Inertial Navigation Contracts for French Nuclear Deterrence
evening.text:
On November 2, 2026, Safran Electronics announced a new contract to provide inertial navigation systems for the French Navy’s submarines.

Safran press release

Safran Electronics & Defense has been selected this year for three inertial navigation programs supporting France’s strategic nuclear deterrence, equipping three main platforms with its HRG (Hemispherical Resonator Gyroscope) technology:

  • Sub-Surface Ballistic Nuclear (SSBN): The Global Navigation System (SGN) for France’s third-generation SSBNs will deliver unmatched performance, enabling extremely long periods of autonomous navigation without any need for GNSS recalibration. This autonomous capability is critical to the SSBN mission—operating underwater without satellite signals, the submarine must navigate discreetly and initialize M51 missile launches independently. This new system will succeed Safran Electronics & Defense’s SGN-3EV, currently in service on Triomphant-class submarines.
  • M51 Missile: Safran Electronics & Defense designs and manufactures the inertial navigation unit for current versions of the M51 missile. For the M51.4, which will equip the 2nd and 3rd generation of the SSBNs, the new CI4 inertial navigation unit will leverage HRG Dual Core technology to provide the missile with enhanced accuracy in a significantly more compact package.
  • Rafale Fighter: The HRG Dual Core technology will also equip most combat aircraft starting from the fifth production batch, featuring the F4 standard. On the aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle, Safran Electronics & Defense’s navigation system serves as a reference for aligning the Rafale’s navigation systems at sea before each mission.

Developed and manufactured in France, the HRG is a high-precision sensor considered as the most advanced inertial sensor in the world. Safran Electronics & Defense invested €120 million this year in its capabilities in France, which currently produces 10,000 HRGs per year and will produce 30,000 units by 2032.

This new achievement extends Safran Electronics & Defense’s more than fifty-year commitment to supporting France’s nuclear deterrence. This commitment was demonstrated once again on October 6: off the coast of Brittany, France, in the presence of the President of the French Republic, the nuclear submarine Le Vigilant successfully launched an M51.3 missile. This test was carried out to validate the operational capability of the ballistic missile submarine after its periodic maintenance and overhaul (IPER). Several of Safran Electronics & Defense’s resilient PNT (Positioning, Navigation and Timing) systems contributed to this success.

On board, the SGN-3EV navigation system and the new BELUGA high-precision clock provided the exact position and time. Inside the missile, the inertial navigation unit ensured extremely accurate guidance. As part of the test operation, the ICARE radar transponders and RGNSS receiver tracked the missile throughout its trajectory from the test center.

“We are particularly proud of the renewed trust shown by the DGA since 1972 in Safran’s navigation and timing solutions. We owe our ability to meet the highest standards and deliver the best possible performance to our teams and our 58 industrial and technological sites, rooted in local regions as well as internationally, which contribute every day to the sovereignty of France and its allies”, said Franck Saudo, President of Safran Electronics & Defense.

– End –

evening.title: The Beechcraft M-346N Is The Only Known Aircraft Left In The Navy’s Jet Trainer Competition
evening.text:
The Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) has decided not to propose its Freedom Jet design for the U.S. Navy’s Undergraduate Jet Training System (UJTS) competition. The field of contenders for UJTS, which aims to find a replacement for the aging T-45 Goshawk jet trainer, has narrowed significantly already this year. The Beechcraft M-346N, put forward by U.S. firm Textron and Italy’s Leonardo, is now the only known major design left in the running.

SNC’s decision on UJTS was first reported by Breaking Defense and has since been further confirmed by Aviation Week. In September, Northrop Grumman had announced it was dropping out of its partnership with SNC on the Freedom Jet proposal. General Atomics has also been named in the past as being part of this team. The Navy’s deadline for bids for its jet trainer competition had come up on October 30. The service’s stated goal has been to acquire 216 new trainers to replace the just under 200 T-45s that are in its inventory today.

“With great respect for the Navy and PMA-273, SNC could not responsibly bid the UJTS program under the current contract structure,” SNC said in a statement to Breaking Defense. “We do remain committed to naval jet training and stand ready to re-engage if the approach is revisited.”

Textron Aviation Defense separately confirmed to that outlet that it submitted the M-346N, a navalized version of the Leonardo-developed M-346 Master advanced jet trainer, and said that it was “ready to support the U.S. Navy and its future training needs.”

TWZ previously flew aboard the M-346, providing a firsthand look at the aircraft Textron is pitching to the service.

Whether or not any other serious bids have been submitted for UJTS is unknown. What impact SNC’s decision not to put forward a proposal may now have on the competition is unclear. TWZ has reached out to SNC and Textron Aviation Defense, as well as the Navy, for additional details.

“Proposals were due on 30 October 2026,” the Navy’s UJTS program office said in response to our queries. “The Government is in source selection with the intent to award the UJTS procurement in 4QFY27 [the fourth quarter of Fiscal Year 2027].”

A competition that has steadily narrowed

As mentioned, SNC’s announcement follows decisions by several other major aerospace companies to pull out of the running for UJTS.

Lockheed Martin announced in April that it would not submit a proposal for UJTS. The company had previously planned to submit the TF-50N, a navalized version of the T-50 developed with Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI). Neither firm appears to have given a detailed explanation for this decision.

Boeing followed suit in June, saying it would not put forward a proposal due to issues tied to the General Electric F404 turbofan and UJTS engine qualification requirements. The company had been expected to submit a bid involving a version of the T-7A Red Hawk being built now for the U.S. Air Force, which is powered by a single F404.

After Boeing’s announcement, the Navy’s competition looked to be down to just two established teams: Textron and Leonardo with the M-346N, and SNC with its Freedom Jet. It is important to note that the M-346N and Freedom Jet are twin-engine aircraft, while the TF-50N and T-7A are single-engine types. SNC had also been the only one in the running with a clean-sheet design.

Now the field has dwindled to just one major contender, the Textron/Leonardo team, at least that we know of, barring the emergence of a surprise entrant. The Navy has not confirmed how many bids it ultimately received for UJTS. The service could also potentially reopen the UJTS competition or otherwise restructure its T-45 replacement plans.

A changing naval aviation training landscape

Since the early 1990s, the Navy has been using variants of the T-45 Goshawk to train future naval aviators destined to fly tactical jets and other carrier-based aircraft. This includes members of the U.S. Marine Corps and foreign student aviators. The Goshawks are currently the service’s only fast jet trainer aircraft.

Despite having received various upgrades over the years, the T-45 fleet continues to age and has faced significant struggles. This includes a spate of reported hypoxia-like physiological episodes among pilots that led to the development of a new oxygen system. There have been several Goshawk crashes in recent years due to a variety of factors, the most recent of which came just this past May. The pilots of that aircraft involved in that mishap thankfully survived.

As such, there has been a growing imperative to replace the T-45s, which led to the UJTS program. UJTS also reflects broader changes to how future naval aviators are trained.

One of the most significant developments already has been the elimination of carrier qualification requirements, including touch-and-goes and full landings, from the syllabus for students in the tactical air aviator training pipeline. Those individuals can still get carrier qualifications in T-45s, if there is time and space available. There is currently still a carrier qualification requirement for future E-2 Hawkeye pilots and foreign student aviators in order to graduate and earn their coveted wings of gold.

At present, prospective naval aviators training to fly fixed-wing carrier-based aircraft do still have to conduct so-called Field Carrier Landing Practice (FCLP) at facilities ashore. FCLP is structured in such a way that it “simulates, as near as practicable, the conditions encountered during carrier landing operations,” per the Navy.

This is all set to change further with the acquisition of new trainers through UJTS. Unlike the T-45, the Navy’s future jet trainers are not required to have features to support full carrier-based operations, touch-and-goes on those ships, or even FCLP training at bases on land.

The Navy’s decision to alter what have long been considered vital aspects of the naval aviator training pipeline has been and continues to be controversial. Concerns and criticisms have been raised about safety and other ramifications of cutting carrier qualification and other requirements.

For its part, the Navy has argued that other modernization efforts have fundamentally changed what is necessary to train naval aviators. The service regularly points to the development of new live, virtual, and constructive training capabilities and associated constructs, as well as assisted carrier landing capabilities, such as Magic Carpet and its successors.

The Navy has also said that the changes help move student aviators through training faster, helping to address chronic pilot shortages. There is a cost-benefit argument to be made here, too.

It is important to note here that with Freedom Jet, SNC had made an explicit and deliberate decision to develop an aircraft that could still perform carrier qualifications and FCLP training. The company said it did so to preserve those capabilities and give the Navy flexibility to alter its naval aviator training plans in the future.

The T-45 replacement schedule continues to slip

Beyond the further narrowing of the field of competitors, the UJTS program has already faced delays and other hurdles. The Navy had originally hoped to see its new jet trainers begin entering service in 2028. That schedule subsequently slipped multiple times. The stated plan earlier this year was to at least award the UJTS contract by March 2027. As mentioned earlier, the contract award timeline has now shifted again to sometime in the fourth quarter of the current fiscal cycle, which runs between next July and September.

Earlier this year, the Navy also confirmed that it had increased the total cost ceiling for the prospective UJTS contract from approximately $1.8 billion to $2.7 billion. “The cost structure has raised concerns as the Navy has detailed an initial award cost of $52.8 million in fiscal 2027 and $181 million for fiscal 2028,” according to Aviation Week’s report today.

With all this in mind, the M-346N does offer an option that is powered by established Honeywell F124 turbofan engines and that can leverage significant existing supply chains. Other versions of the M-346 are already in service with multiple air forces globally, and more operators are on the horizon.

At the same time, SNC’s withdrawal and other prior setbacks for the UJTS program can only raise questions about how the competition might now proceed with only one major entrant left. SNC’s statement to Breaking Defense makes clear the company is willing to re-engage with the Navy if there is a further shake-up in the T-45 replacement plans.

For the Navy, acquiring a successor to the T-45 is only becoming an ever-more pressing priority. That being said, with how the UJTS effort has already proceeded to date, another change of tack cannot be entirely ruled out.

evening.title: Bare metal boom: On-prem server sales for HPC and AI up 20% this year
evening.text:
On-premises high-performance compute (HPC) is still in demand, according to Hyperion Research, which estimates the market is expanding at almost 20 percent year-on-year, often driven by requirements for AI processing.

What Hyperion calls the "on-premises HPC and AI-for-Science" server market showed significant growth in the first half of 2026, with revenues hitting $16.5 billion, up 19.9 percent.

However, the analyst says unit shipments over the same period grew only 4.4 percent, meaning that systems are carrying a higher price tag due to greater use of costly components such as GPUs and other accelerators, not to mention the effects of higher memory costs, which have tripled or quadrupled since last year.

Its tracking of the HPC market is based on multiple surveys conducted of both buyers and suppliers, the firm says. The latest data shows a major change in the overall HPC market growth, heavily driven by a combination of the use of AI, large language models (LLMs), and purchases of large GPU/accelerator-based systems.

This trend was noted a couple of years ago, with Omdia reporting in 2024 that revenue growth from server sales was racing ahead of actual units shipped, as customers prioritized investment in highly configured server clusters for AI.

Much of that spending was by hyperscalers and cloud providers, seeking to profit from selling AI services to enterprise customers, but Hyperion’s figures focus on on-prem shipments, showing that many enterprises prefer to do their processing in-house.

According to Hyperion, Dell has now surpassed HPE as the biggest HPC vendor, with server revenues of $4.2 billion for the first half of 2026. HPE, which picked up supercomputing specialist Cray for $1.3 billion in 2019, had long been pack leader in the global HPC arena in terms of market share and revenue.

The figures put Dell on a 24 percent share, while HPE is not far behind on 21 percent. Lenovo and China-based Sugon trail behind at 4 percent share each, while 45 percent of the market is just labelled as "others" by Hyperion. This includes names such as Bull, which re-emerged from the shadows of Atos this year, plus Supermicro, Penguin Computing, and NEC.

The HPC infrastructure market is inherently cyclical. HPE recognized significant revenue in 2025 with sales of multiple exascale-class leadership machines, but procurement of that scale is intermittent and doesn't necessarily come along every year, Hyperion notes.

"Organizations and institutions are continuing to invest in their advanced computing infrastructure due to both replacing aging machines and the desire to adopt AI into their workflows to support their businesses and missions," said Hyperion Research CEO Earl Joseph.

"The growth reflects both a nominal increase in units being purchased and significant increases in system prices."

HPC systems are considered the backbone for many AI and AI-related applications, which has driven the overall HPC market to a new growth level, Joseph added. ®

evening.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
evening.text:
I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.  

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level. 

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.

Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout. 

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4. 

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

evening.title: VMware returns to low-end server virtualization with 'vSphere Express'
evening.text:
As first reported by The Register, VMware has returned to the low-end server virtualization market with a product called "vSphere Express."

The product will run on up to 128 processor cores and includes vMotion to allow live migration of VMs, automated restart of failed VMs, a distributed switch, rapid non-disruptive patching, and support for physical and virtual trusted platform modules.

"We have been listening to the market at the low end, and they want a basic core server virtualization platform," said Prashanth Shenoy, vice president of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). He explained that each instance of vSphere Express will be discrete, meaning it won't be possible to manage them centrally.

"This is tested for small implementations," he told The Register. "We do not want a customer to run this on thousands of cores." Shenoy said the vSphere Foundation (VVF) enterprise virtualization product, and Cloud Foundation (VCF) private cloud suite, are appropriate for users with more complex needs. vSphere Express will, however, match the release cadence of VVF and VCF.

Under Broadcom’s ownership, VMware has enormously reduced the number of resellers in its channel program, meaning it no longer has partners who are a good fit for this product.

The virtualization giant will therefore sell vSphere Express through its distributors, most of which now operate cloud marketplaces at which affiliated resellers can acquire software – an arrangement channel folk call "two tier distribution."

We asked VMware to tell us the price it will charge for vSphere Express.

A spokesperson told us it will offer a per-core subscription license at a price "significantly lower" than VVF or VCF but declined to quote a dollar amount. "We encourage interested customers to reach out to their local reseller for information related to pricing and subscription terms," the spokesperson wrote.

VMware has also bulked out VVF and VCF a little, by adding disaster recovery and policy-based networking for virtual private clouds that it previously sold as add-ons. Shenoy pitched the additions as demonstrating VMware's intention to add value to VVF and VCF, in part by ensuring the bundles include tools that users are likely to consider represent essential functionality.

The Broadcom business unit will also add new features, such as native AWS S3-compatible object storage for its VSAN virtual storage. That update, due in calendar Q1 of 2027, means VSAN will become a more convenient platform on which to store the unstructured data that AI workloads rely on, therefore boosting the utility of VMware's AI Factory.

VMware also plans to make its AI Factory easier to implement.

"The idea is to focus more on AI, less on setup," Shenoy said.

Analysis: A welcome low-end return faces an uncertain reception

VMware's return to the low-end server virtualization market may not be well-received, because it has largely ignored users of its existing low-end vSphere Standard product for the last few years, and irritated many by insisting they upgrade to the more expensive and complex VCF.

The virtualization giant also cast aside thousands of resellers.

When The Register chats with members of the VMware community, we often hear that trust in the vendor has diminished.

Your correspondent therefore feels that vSphere Express will get a mixed reception.

Many vSphere Standard users will welcome a more appropriate and affordable upgrade option, especially as it means they won't need to learn new skills.

Other users and former partners will wonder if, having been bitten by Broadcom once, they should now be a little shy of vSphere Express.

Broadcom shareholders should be enthusiastic, as VMware's decision not to sell to the low end of the market blocked its onramp to new users. The chips 'n' code shop now has another way to get VMware growing, if it can restore trust. ®

evening.title: India’s Aditya-L1 Sees Something Unusual in a Solar Eruption
evening.text:
India’s first space-based solar observatory, Aditya-L1 has helped scientists take a peek into the nature of expansion of a solar eruption or a coronal mass eruption (CME) and gain new insights into it. This could be important for space-weather studies and thereby affecting our satellites and communication networks.
Aditya L 1 satellite launched in September 2023 is now operational at the Sun–Earth L1 point, providing continuous observations of the Sun. It carries 7 payloads, of which the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), the primary payload, is an internally occulted coronagraph designed to observe the solar corona simultaneously in various modes.
By combining data from the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph on Aditya-L1 with complementary observations from NASA’s SDO spacecraft and three-dimensional modeling, scientists from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), an autonomous institution of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) were able to reconstruct the full 3-D geometry and dynamics of solar eruptions.
Their study published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, showed, for the first time, that the CME did not expand outward from the Sun like a simple symmetric bubble, as previously thought. Instead, it underwent non-uniform expansion and developed an asymmetric shape. These differences in CME expansion can affect its speed as it travels towards Earth causing space-weather disturbances.
The VELC studies nascent CMEs through spectroscopy in the 530.3 nm wavelength green emission line due to highly ionized iron atoms in the corona. This line emission captures hot coronal plasma which is at temperatures of around 1.8 million Kelvin. The Doppler shift, or the change in the wavelength of this emission line provides information about plasma velocity along the line of sight, and close to the solar disk.
The VELC, with this unique capability, was designed and fabricated by the IIA at its MGK Menon Lab for Space Sciences on the CREST campus in Hosakote, with substantial support from ISRO.
“We observed the CME that occurred on 5 August 2024 using the VELC as well as data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) onboard NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO)”, explained Saurabh Tripathi, a PhD student at IIA, and lead author of the study. The CME was launched from an active region near the western limb of the Sun. VELC’s spectroscopic data show an unusual yet distinct Doppler pattern of blueward and red-ward shifted emission, which arises from plasma moving towards and away from us, respectively.
“Our results show that the CME did not expand uniformly. The AIA images captured how the CME propagated across the sky, while VELC revealed the motion of the expanding CME bubble towards and away from us,” Tanmoy Samanta, a solar astronomer at IIA and the corresponding author of the study elaborated. Together, these observations reveal that the CME did not expand like a simple spherical bubble. Instead, its uneven expansion caused it to develop an asymmetric shape.
“To understand the unusual spectral pattern observed by VELC, we then developed a 3-D geometric-kinematic model of an expanding CME”, said Jayant Joshi of IIA and a co-author. The model was used to test how the CME’s orientation and uneven sideways expansion could produce the spectral structures observed by VELC. A model with symmetric expansion could not reproduce the observed pattern. Instead, a model of an inclined CME axis and asymmetric lateral expansion produced a spectral pattern and temporal evolution similar to those observed by VELC. The researchers plan to use this technique on other CMEs, to reconstruct their motion without relying entirely on multi-viewpoint imaging from telescopes in space. This complementarity is particularly valuable in the lower corona, where CMEs evolve rapidly, and their motion along the line of sight cannot be obtained from imaging alone.

evening.title: US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
evening.text:
He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday.

A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023.

These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents.

Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems.

Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files.

The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021.

It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so.

On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents.

Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings.

The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only.

Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket.

On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023.

Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began.

The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters.

Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia.

Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors.

According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information.

Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government.

Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023.

The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials.

On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000.

"Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.

"By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

evening.text:
In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain.

Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die.

Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. They went on to discover that mice using the chemical did not develop a high tolerance for it and that mice already dependent on morphine—a powerful opioid—could consume SR-17018 to reset their tolerance without suffering from painful withdrawal symptoms.

evening.title: PushpakO2 Showcases Mothership-Swarm UAV Concept
evening.text:
Indian aerospace and advanced engineering firm PushpakO2 has revealed details of its concept for a mothership swarm UAV system. The mothership is designed to deploy small autonomous loitering UAVs. The Bhopal based company states the project is currently in research and prototyping phase.
The concept art shows a larger UAV deploying multiple smaller fixed wing UAVs. The Mothership is an autonomous AI driven UAV for precision strike capability. The mothership will have the capability to deploy UAVs from the mothership, incorporate AI, encrypted communications and scalable design. The images are concept art and the mothership design is an aspiration.
The main concept behind the mothership is to have a larger UAV which can carry multiple smaller UAVs. This can give more flexibility with the mission objectives. As the smaller UAVs can be deployed from the Mothership.
This could provide more flexibility with the UAVs as they can all be launched from a single UAV. The smaller UAVs could each have different roles depending on the weapons, sensors and software they carry.
The smaller UAVs are loitering UAVs. The concept uses multiple autonomous systems to work together. The mothership does not state how many UAVs it could carry, how far it could go, how long it could stay on station, how much it could carry or how autonomous it would be in operations. The Mothership concept brings together multiple technologies, including the flight control system for the mothership, release system, autonomous navigation for the smaller UAVs and communications.
Encrypted communications could help track progress of the mission and send commands. But how well it works depends on the robustness of the system and how it handles communication issues, navigation issues and unexpected situations for individual UAVs.
The AI driven aspect does not guarantee the UAVs can target and identify targets autonomously. The drones’ autonomy is not specified in the description.
As this is intended for use in contested environments, it will be important that the system is robust, secure, resilient to navigation issues and clear that humans have control over the weapon systems. Mothership launched UAVs are gaining interest around the world. They provide an alternative way to launch UAVs. The Mothership can increase the range of the smaller UAVs and means they do not need to be launched from individual locations.
In India these concepts could be used alongside traditional UAVs and loitering weapons. But how useful they are will depend on how well they perform, cost, how easy they are to maintain and if they can integrate with current military command and control systems.
The concept from PushpakO2 shows how Indian private companies are getting involved in advanced aerospace projects. However the project is still in research and prototyping stages. The concept art should not be seen as an operational capability.

evening.title: HP Inc hires former GSK boss as CEO
evening.text:
HP Inc has hired former GSK boss Emma Walmsley to plot its course through choppy PC and print waters.

Walmsley spent eight years as the boss at pharma biz GSK and further back in time held various marketing and general management positions at L'Oreal. She has no track record running a tech company, though she was on Microsoft’s board.

“Throughout the process, Emma stood out for the strength of her leadership experience across multiple industries, the clarity of her strategic thinking and her ability to translate customer insights into new growth,” said Chip Bergh, chair of HP's board.

In the first nine months of HP's fiscal 2026, revenue had jumped 10 percent year-on-year to $44.5 billion. The print business shrank in that time and PCs generated the growth. However, amid a memory crunch with supplies dwindling, analysts are forecasting PC market contraction in terms of unit sales.

Global PC shipments slumped 20 percent in Q3 as DRAM shortages forced up prices and customers opted instead to sweat their assets rather than replace their fleet of computers. Things aren't expected to improve in the final three months of 2026.

One beacon of hope for all PC makers was AI, yet many customers aren't buying into the story for various reasons.

Walmsley previously said that during her time at the top of GSK she created a "totally different company, in platform, in momentum, in talent, in culture," she told the FT. "I think in time… it will be recognized." She also dealt with activist investor Elliot Management, which operates in the tech industry and called for her to reapply for the CEO role at GSK, claiming her lack of science background was an issue.

Walmsley said: "HP is an iconic company with a defining role in shaping the future of work on a global scale. I’m excited to join the team and, together, move forward with clarity and conviction. We will focus on harnessing the power of the AI era and putting HP’s creativity and innovation to work to unlock new sources of growth and deliver lasting value for our customers, shareholders, partners and people."

Employees will be crossing their fingers that their new boss doesn’t borrow from the playbook of her predecessor - who hotfooted it to PayPal in February - by running multiple redundancy rounds, and shareholders will hope their stock price show sustainable improvement. If not, Walmsley may have to manage more interest from activist investors at the latest corporation she is running. ®

evening.title: Pakistan’s HQ-19 Interest Linked to India’s Growing SSBN Fleet : Pakistani Analyst
evening.text:
Pakistan may be working towards gaining access to China’s advanced HQ-19 anti-ballistic missile system after satellite imagery highlighted potential Chinese CETC long-range radar installations in the nation.
Pakistani defence analyst Bilal Khan wrote in an analysis on November 2, “The radar sightings appear to be CETC’s SLC-12/SLC-14 long range radar systems from China Electronics Technology Group Corporation (CETC). If true, it could indicate Pakistan is preparing to create a more advanced missile defence system based around the Chinese HQ-19”.China has been investing in its long-range radar systems to support its increasingly sophisticated air and missile defence systems. Several new and improved radar systems were displayed at the Airshow China 2024 event including the ‘780’ target designation radar and ‘610A’ intelligence radar.
Both radars are to support China’s HQ-19 air and missile defence system, with the former used for air defence and anti-missile capabilities and the latter being intelligence and surveillance.
The HQ-19 is intended to intercept ballistic missile threats, which can be extremely fast and have a high altitude.
If there are any indications that there are Chinese radars in Pakistan, it would be a key indicator that there is potential for the equipment to be used in establishing a ballistic missile defence system. However, it is currently unclear what type of radar has been installed.
Khan claims Pakistan’s interest in ballistic missile defence can be linked to its concern over India’s increasing sea-based nuclear capabilities, specifically their nuclear propelled ballistic missile submarines.
The Arihant-class submarines give India a second strike capability, as they can now deploy their nuclear armed ballistic missiles from underwater. This can cause concern for Pakistan if there are more SSBNs introduced and the missiles become more advanced.
Statements made by retired Lieutenant General Khalid Kidwai, an adviser to Pakistan’s National Command Authority, regarding the threat from India’s SSBN capabilities, could indicate an increasing interest in developing defensive capabilities.
However, Pakistan would face a large challenge in creating an equivalent nuclear powered ballistic missile submarine. A ballistic missile defence system could be a way in which Islamabad could address some of its concerns. However, it would not fully solve the issue.
The acquisition of the HQ-19 would be a large step forward in Pakistan’s air defence capabilities. They already have several Chinese radars including the HQ-9/P and other long and medium range Surface-to-Air Missiles.
However, the HQ-19 would be used for a different purpose, to intercept ballistic missiles at a much higher altitude. It would rely on a network of surveillance radars, tracking systems, command facilities and interceptor launchers.

evening.title: Aswath Damodaran trims his Anthropic IPO valuation to $1.45 trillion; Dean of valuation explains why
evening.text: Valuation expert Aswath Damodaran trimmed his valuation estimate for AI giant Anthropic to $1.45 trillion, from his earlier estimate of $1.475 trillion which was already lower than the industry estimates of $2 trillion.The 'Dean of Valuation' in a long blogpost said his earlier valuation estimate which was lower than the overall market view received strong reactions. Some of them were solely based on emotion, he said, as they held strong conviction in the company. Some of it was based on cost of capital, which the analyst believes reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and basic business sense.Also read | Dean of valuation Aswath Damodaran pegs Anthropic's worth at $1.475 trillion ahead of mega IPOHis latest $1.45 trillion valuation accounts for the trailing 12-month revenue and operating income numbers to include the just-leaked third quarter numbers. “The equity value that I obtain for Anthropic is close to the lower end of the offering price estimates, but as I noted at the time that I posted it, and will reinforce again now, it is a function of not just my upbeat story about the company, but also one about how the AI products and services market will evolve over time,” he wrote.Aswath Damodaran’s worries for AnthropicDamodaran estimates Anthropic’s target revenues will reach a trillion dollars in ten years. Not only would this put them at or close to the top of all companies, in terms of total annual revenues, but they will also be sharing that grouping with companies like Amazon and Walmart that deliver on scale, but at the expense of margins, he said, adding that Anthropic emerges as a winner in the premium portion of the AI market, capturing a dominant market share, with pricing power.In his previous post valuing Anthropic, Damodaran had raised the alarm over the company’s governance structure, stating that its structure as a public benefit corporation and a voting share concoction that leaves founders in control, no matter how much capital the company raises in equity markets. He said he received feedback that this may not be a negative as these are smart people who know AI better than the rest. The analyst is however not convinced as he believes concentration of power in the hands of founders is a bad idea.Also read | Aswath Damodaran explains why country risk is no longer just an emerging market problem“While much of the focus on Anthropic has been on their compute commitments, disclosed (loosely) in their prospectus, my valuation of Anthropic is driven by expectations of what those commitments will look like over time, and especially if my growth story for the company comes into fruition. Delivering a trillion dollars of revenues will require Anthropic to not just maintain and replenish the compute power that it has already locked down, but add to that power over time,” Damodaran said, warning that building new data centers is getting more difficult, as local communities push back, and politicians realize that opposing them is a net vote winnerRegulatory risks are also one of the key worries for Anthropic. “Put simply, Anthropic will become riskier, if revenues do not measure up to expectations and the pathway to profitability becomes rockier, making it more an output than an input variable,” the valuation expert said.How investors should react to Anthropic’s IPO?While Damodaran remains cautious about Anthropic’s IPO, he noted that uncertainty is a feature of investing, no matter what one invests in, with the differences across investments lying in how much uncertainty one face, rather than whether she faces.Also read | AI boom heading for a dot-com-style bust? ‘Dean of Valuation’ Aswath Damodaran warns correction could be more painful than 2008He listed out four responses to such uncertainties.1) Ignore it: Damodaran pointed out that there are investors who are capable of ignoring uncertainty and going in fully even on the most uncertain investments. They are able to do so because they are far less risk averse than the rest and are willing to live with the consequences of investments (and their portfolios) blowing up. “They are more gamblers than investors, but with good instincts and timing, gamblers can get wealthy too,” he said.2) Avoid it: If an investor completely wants to avoid uncertainty, she cannot invest in equities, corporate bonds, which have risk of default, and even treasury bonds, which have price risk from shifting interest rates, Damodaran noted. Unless the investor simply wants to just hold cash, she has to therefore decide what her threshold for risk is, and stay within that threshold.3) Margin of Safety: The third approach to dealing with uncertainty also borrows from conventional value investing and imposing a margin of safety, where you will buy a stock only if its price is less than your value estimate by a margin (20%, 30%, 40%) that you specify.4) Law of large numbers: “If I had a million dollars in investable funds, would I invest that entire amount in Anthropic, even if it trades at well below my assessed value? The answer would be no, given the uncertainties associated with the future of the company, but that answer would change if my portfolio became less concentrated, since its performance would be less a function of any individual company's performance (good or bad),” Damodaran said. In effect, he said he is using the law of large numbers as an ally to not only reduce his risk exposure to individual companies, but also as a basis for making investments in far riskier stocks than he would be otherwise inclined to invest in.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Debaroti Adhikary, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. US midterm candidates find something to agree on: Reining in datacenters
evening.text:
Datacenter restrictions found broad support among candidates for governor in this week's US midterm elections, with nearly all those examined by Data Center Watch backing bans, pauses, or tighter development rules.

Data Center Watch, which tracks grassroots opposition to compute sheds across America, examined the public positions of 74 selected candidates across the 36 states that elected governors in the midterm elections on November 3.

It found that 43 percent of those candidates supported a ban or moratorium on new projects, while another 51 percent backed further regulation or conditional development. Only about 5 percent had no stated public position.

Support for bans or moratoriums crossed party lines, although it was more common among the Democratic candidates examined (60 percent) than Republicans (30 percent).

Candidates from both major parties backed restrictions in eight states: Maryland, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon, Wisconsin, and Texas.

Texas has experienced a boom in data campus development recently, thanks to its ample energy resources and light-touch regulations, although outgoing governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause earlier this year while audits of energy and water use were carried out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Abbott in Tuesday's election and will take office in January.

Those positions matter to developers because governors can shape state regulation, energy policy, and permitting, although approval powers vary by jurisdiction.

However, temporary pauses and targeted construction restrictions do not necessarily amount to opposition to all datacenter development.

Things were even starker where folk got to vote directly on the issue, with measures regarding datacenters appearing on the ballot as well as candidates. Data Centers on the Ballot, which tracked many of these, found that 43 out of 46 municipalities where tighter restrictions on server farms were up for a vote had approved those at the time of publication. Only in one case, the City of Harwood in North Dakota, had restrictions been rejected, and 2 had yet to post results.

AI-related campaign spending has also come under scrutiny. Guardrails Alliance, a labor-backed pressure group, described Leading the Future, a super PAC network opposing AI regulation, as "largely a non-factor" in the elections. It alleged the network avoided the most competitive races because "they know their money is politically toxic."

Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the US in response to the facilities popping up in people's backyards, often without them having any say in the process.

A Gallup survey earlier this year discovered that more than 70 percent of Americans would be against the construction of one in their neighborhood, while a Pew Research Center survey found that Americans increasingly believe datacenters are bad for the environment and blame them for rising household energy bills.

Pew also found that advertisers spent almost $12 million on Facebook and Instagram political ads mentioning datacenters between July 27 and October 24. Among those running in October through the study's cutoff, 57 percent opposed datacenters and just three percent supported them.

Common themes included corporate interests, energy use, environmental effects, and water consumption. ®

evening.title: C-130J vs C-390: Which Is Better for Indian Navy MPA?
evening.text:
If the Indian Navy goes for either the C-130J or Embraer C-390 for their future MPA, the SC-130J derivative would provide a clearer route to a full ASW aircraft. While the C-390 may provide a faster maritime surveillance and ASW platform, a similar configuration has not been shown for the proposed patrol version.
Not only does the platform need to be equipped with surveillance radar and cameras, but detection of submarines, the ability to deploy sonobuoys, acoustic data processing and torpedo delivery could be key for the Indian Navy.
An agreement was signed between Embraer and the Brazilian Air Force in December 2024 to investigate the intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities of the C-390. These studies were joined by Portugal in April 2025. The studies should be completed by the end of 2026. However, Embraer will still need to find a launch customer.
The proposed aircraft will have a modular mission system which can be used for transport and other functions. Concept art shows a surveillance pod, synthetic aperture radar and electro-optical and infrared sensor. This will also have advanced communication systems and the ability to launch anti-ship missiles.
However, there has not been a full ASW system announced. Sonobuoy launchers, acoustic data processing, magnetic anomaly detection and torpedo delivery will need to be specified. The C-390 should be seen as a developing maritime surveillance aircraft at this stage.
The SC-130J Sea Hercules proposed by Lockheed Martin provides three different levels of capability. It has been published that the aircraft will be able to be upgraded from maritime surveillance to anti-surface warfare and a full ASW platform. The highest level of capability has sonobuoy deployment, acoustic data processing, torpedoes, and a magnetic anomaly detection system.
However, the aircraft has not been operationalised. The US Coast Guard have a fleet of HC-130J aircraft that show the potential for maritime surveillance, but this does not prove the full ASW capability of the SC-130J. The C-390 does have the benefit of being a faster aircraft to get to remote patrol areas. It also has a modern cabin and modular design. The C-130J, however, has four turbo prop engines and would be an interesting choice due to its proposed ASW configuration. It will also provide longer patrol times and the ability to fly at lower speeds.
The C-130Js are also in use by the Indian Air Force which may provide training and logistical benefits. However, a naval mission system would need to be integrated, tested and certified separately.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat 

In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat.

Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.

Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.

Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef.

—Meghan McCarron

This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration

More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that.

It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.

This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

evening.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
evening.text:
A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

evening.title: Watchdog sticks probe into Capita's handling of 1.7 million member civil service pension scheme
evening.text:
Capita has repeatedly "broken" promises to resolve the "chaos" engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) following its takeover of the administration – a move that left thousands of retired public sector workers unpaid.

So says Parliamentary spending watchdog, the Public Accounts Committee, which this week launched an inquiry into the handover of the ten-year £239 million contract in December from previous incumbent MyCSP.

As The Register exclusively revealed, the troubles began early on as members of CSPS – which manages pensions for 1.7 million people – complained of unrecognized passwords and usernames on the portal Capita developed. Capita said it inherited 132,100 complex remediation cases, and claimed the work-in-progress backlog from the prior system was more than double the 37,000 items when it won the deal in 2023.

Capita ran to Microsoft for support, and promised the use AI and automation, in addition to its 500 full-time employees working on the project, would resolve the issues by March. It missed this deadline, as well as one set for June 30 and is set to miss March 2027.

The government subsequently withheld a £10 million payment to Capita over the CSPS fiasco.

The National Audit Office, a spending regulator, has already launched its own probe into the failures and is now joined by the PAC, which says thousands of civil servants and their families have struggled to on and collect their pensions

The PAC has already held three evidence sessions on Capita and the government’s efforts to ameliorate the situation. The law was changed in the Budget 2026 to mitigate the impact of administrative delays in CSPS on bereaved families.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair at the PAC, said in a statement:

"In response to the alarming reports of hard-working civil servants being thrown into financial uncertainty following Capita’s takeover of the CSPS, we have held a number of evidence sessions with both the top leadership of Capita, and the civil servants and ministers of the Cabinet Office who have ultimate responsibility for overseeing the contract.

"Over and over again, promises have been made and broken by Capita, to our faces in formal evidence sessions, that they will get a grip on what has gone wrong. As a result, we are launching an inquiry, which will be informed by the authoritative factual basis provided by the NAO, which supports the scrutiny work of this Committee."

The inquiry will draw on the finding of the NAO's forthcoming report on the switch of CSPS to Capita, and will take into consideration the status of the scheme at go-live date, how Capita has performed, and the effect on CSPS members, plus take a look into the way the Cabinet Office has overseen the prior scheme and the switch to Capita. ®

Updated to add at 1407 UTC:
Capita has been in touch to say how "deeply sorry" it is about the "frustration" that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme "has caused members and their families."
It said it had "made progress," but had a lot more to do. It said its teams are working to resolve outstanding cases "as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

evening.title: Cyberattack on French plasma stores is enough to make your blood boil
evening.text:
Attackers tampered with cold-storage settings used by France's civilian blood service after compromising a refrigeration supplier, the organization said.

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed the incident on Tuesday, saying its own systems had not been directly targeted. Safeguards prevented any loss of blood products.

The affected equipment stored blood samples and frozen plasma, including plasma intended for transfusion.

"The EFS' monitoring and alarm systems enabled the rapid identification of these anomalies and the implementation of necessary measures to ensure that no blood samples or products were compromised," it said.

"Thus, depending on the circumstances, as soon as the incident occurred, the affected equipment was either brought under control without impacting the products and samples, or neutralized; the products stored in these cold rooms were preventively transferred to other facilities."

The EFS did not name the supplier publicly.

According to reports, attackers changed cold-room temperature settings from -30°C to 110°C. That does not mean the equipment or its contents reached the higher temperature.

The organization added that it notified the country's cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the Ministry of Health.

News about cyberattacks targeting refrigeration devices across Europe emerged on Monday morning after retailers arrived to work, only to find puddles on the floor after cyber criminals activated defrost modes.

Reports of the supermarket attacks describe remotely activated defrost cycles and temperatures as high as 50°C, forcing retailers to discard spoiled food.

The attackers have not been identified. More retailers have reported disruption since the initial disclosures on Monday.

Stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden were the first to report issues, although cases from Estonia, Finland, Germany, Portugal, Romania, and the Netherlands have since been confirmed.

Richard Horne, chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told BBC Radio 4's Today program on Wednesday that he was aware of "a couple of impacts" in the UK's own food supply chain.

No affected UK businesses have publicly identified themselves, although the British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC that some of its more than 300 members had become "collateral" in the attacks, with two reporting that their fridges had begun defrosting.

The latest wave of cold-store attacks comes a month after the first, which affected French supermarket chains Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others.

Both supermarket waves involved remote interference with refrigeration controls, causing stock losses. Whether the attack affecting EFS used the same access route remains unclear.

Some affected chains identified Danfoss controllers in their systems; others said they did not use the company's equipment.

CERT-FR published an advisory at the time of the attacks urging organizations to remediate vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers.

The attacks in France followed reports of compromises at US military commissaries, which also led to food wastage in August. ®

evening.title: Achieving nirvana: Enlightenment 0.28 hits the desktop
evening.text:
Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school.

Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme.

Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too.

This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around.

Trinity is back

The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7, with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray."

Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023. ®

evening.title: Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices
evening.text:
Microsoft wants enterprise customers to start thinking about PC refreshes using the same mindset – and line in the budget – as AI investments. The problem? Rising component costs caused by the proliferation of AI datacenters mean many clients are delaying client refreshes.

In a call to arms, Microsoft became the headline sponsor of the Canalys Forum in Barcelona early last month for the first time ever. Redmond needs distributors and resellers that convene at the event annually to get behind Copilot, Cowork and, more generally, AI computers.

Mark Linton, corporate veep for Windows and Device Sales, took to the stage to preach to a room he is hoping to convert.

"What we're seeing is the tokenomics of [AI] is getting very challenging," he said. "Having agents working on frontier models quickly becomes very expensive."

Redmond's proposed solution is to use those massive LLMs where most needed, "the right model for the right job," running smaller models locally at the edge on Windows PCs. "My goal, if we're successful in pivoting Windows to the agentic platform, is to have PC spend be part of the AI spend versus just PC refresh budget," he said.

"In an AI hybrid world, you'll be able to use edge devices, powerful PCs with lots of memory, lots of capability to run your AI workloads that are appropriate right there on the device. You keep the data locally. Of course, you don't have the token cost of the cloud. You have better latency, and you have more control."

Copilot is merely a component. This is not only about customers using Microsoft "first-party software" – it's for all models and all agents to use Windows as the platform, added Linton.

Goodness knows, Windows does need a shot in the arm. Microsoft last week reported profit and loss accounts for Q1 of its fiscal 2027, ended September 30, and revenue in the Windows OEM and Devices division shrank 22 percent from last year to $3.55 billion. Microsoft warned revenue generated in its Q2 may be down 30 percent.

"Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand and a prior year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support," Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on an earnings call.

Market watcher IDC said calendar Q3 PC shipments sank to 62.7 million units, down 20.1 percent year-on-year, translating into 15.8 million fewer sales into distributors' warehouses. Tough macroeconomic conditions coupled with rising memory costs mean tough times for the PC industry.

Omdia – which owns Canalys – said: "The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly."

Reg readers know why component costs are going up. The datacenter construction frenzy meant memory chip makers could make more money from higher-margin HBM than conventional DRAM, prompting them to prioritize production of the former.

But AI PCs have been a tough sell from the start, as higher prices and a lack of killer applications meant many customers delayed purchases. Microsoft has to convince the market of the benefits – including trade customers as well as those in charge of procurement at enterprises.

Once more, the pitch for AI PCs

Back at the Canalys Forum, Microsoft's Linton claimed customers mulling AI PC purchases want better productivity, to reduce costs, to innovate, and to be able to use these computers securely and at scale.

Microsoft is going to invest heavily in Windows from both the platform capability and security to enable these ends. So, if you are a Microsoft partner, you'll be able to run Windows and secure agents at the operating system level with Agent 365, with Intune, or with Entra.

Linton added: "We announced in June some of the technology in Windows, in particular Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC). And so essentially you can virtualize agents, and then you can use Intune to give them policy. And so other platforms, you have to manage agent by agent. Windows, you'll be able to do it policy-based, much like you manage people and network resources.

"You will have agents for all, and you need to know how to manage them, track them, audit them, and then ensure that they're contained in the right way. So we're doing that at the operating system primitive level."

Some of the quality control issues that have dogged Windows may give some sysadmins pause for thought about the grand claims made by the Windows exec.

Still, Microsoft is on a mission, and it knows how to attract thousands of resellers by dangling financial incentives in their direction. Linton said it is pumping money into channel programs, including AI-readiness funded headcount with "top partners" to "get this hybrid AI story moving."

Microsoft wants the channel to deploy AI internally too, "especially for your sales team" because "if they're using it, they're able to sell it."

Dell isn’t hopeful of an uplift in PC demand this year. David Kennedy, chief financial officer, said sales will remain "compressed."

"The reality is most enterprises this year for their IT budgets are sweating those assets out a little bit more and what dollars they have, they're trying to build out their infrastructure side," he told the Citi TMT conference in September.

"As we go forward, I think you'll see it [become] a little bit more robust. Our main focus will be on those higher ASP (average sales price) commercial boxes as part of the AI storyboard that's there."

He reckons there are more than 400 million PCs owned by customers that are "over four years old", and with the "cheapest token being closest to the data, none of those installed base PCs will have the battery life or the power to do AI workloads on them. So there is a pent-up demand that we believe will come once it stabilizes and once IT budgets get a little bit more settled and expanded."

Will 2027 be the year of the AI desktop? The Reg suspects not, though readers can do what they always do and speak their brains in the comments section. ®
